From "Chrom" Incorporation Numbers An incorporation number, more often called a Federal Tax Identification Number (TIN) or an Employer Identification Number (EIN), is the federal number assigned to a business by the Internal Revenue Service. The Internal Revenue Service requires every corporation or partnership to have one. The number is used by the federal government to identify the business for tax reporting purposes. Most businesses, depending on legal structure, will also need the number for such things as opening a business checking account, obtaining business credit or hiring employees. Like a Social Security number for individuals, each incorporation number assigned is unique and is issued exclusively to that particular business.

Requirements Corporations and partnerships are required to have an incorporation number, but the Internal Revenue Service requires any business to have an incorporation number if certain criteria apply. If the company has employees, it must obtain an incorporation number. A company must also obtain a number if it participates in a Keogh plan. If the company withholds taxes on income, other than wages, paid to a non-resident alien, it must obtain an incorporation number. If the business files Employment, Excise, or Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms tax returns, or if the company is a certain type of organization, such as a nonprofit or a farmers' cooperative, it must obtain a number as well.
